name: Space-Efficient Exact Algorithms for Subset Sum (reduced-space Schroeppel-Shamir family)
description: A line of work on exact worst-case Subset Sum that preserves the Schroeppel-Shamir O*(2^{0.5n}) time bound while pushing the space usage down. Schroeppel and Shamir (FOCS 1979) solved n-integer Subset Sum in O*(2^{0.5n}) time and O*(2^{0.25n}) space. Nederlof and Wegrzycki (STOC 2021) gave the first space improvement, to O*(2^{0.249999n}), by combining the representation technique (Howgrave-Graham-Joux) with a new reduction to and algorithm for Orthogonal Vectors. Belova, Chukhin, Kulikov and Mihajlin (ESA 2024) further reduce the space to O*(2^{0.246n}) and simplify the algorithm by filtering the family of subsets with a random prime (an idea of Howgrave-Graham and Joux) and then running Schroeppel-Shamir's sorted sum enumeration inside the representation technique, reducing one Subset Sum instance to many instances of Weighted Orthogonal Vectors. In parallel, a polynomial-space line solves Subset Sum in exponential time: Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas (SODA 2018) get O*(2^{0.86n}) time with poly(n, log t) space (assuming random read-only access to random bits); Kane (2010) gave a log-space algorithm with e^{O(n^3 t + n^{2.025} t^{1.025})} time; Jin and Vyas (SODA 2021) give fast low-space algorithms with explicit time-space tradeoffs.
worst_case_time: O*(2^{0.5n}) for the reduced-space algorithms (Belova et al. ESA 2024; Nederlof-Wegrzycki STOC 2021), matching Schroeppel-Shamir FOCS 1979. The polynomial-space line has much larger time: O*(2^{0.86n}) (Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas SODA 2018), while Chen-Jin-Randolph-Servedio (APPROX/RANDOM 2023) give O(2^{n/2} * n^{-0.5023}) time, the first sub-2^{n/2} worst-case time for classical meet-in-the-middle.
space_complexity: O*(2^{0.246n}) for Belova-Chukhin-Kulikov-Mihajlin (ESA 2024), improving O*(2^{0.249999n}) (Nederlof-Wegrzycki STOC 2021) and O*(2^{0.25n}) (Schroeppel-Shamir FOCS 1979). Polynomial-space algorithms use poly(n, log t) space (Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas 2018) or O(log(nt)) space (Kane 2010).
model: Randomized word RAM / unit-cost RAM. The reduced-space algorithms use the representation technique plus modular hashing. Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas assume random read-only access to exponentially many random bits (and poly(n, log t) space). Kane's log-space algorithm works in a Turing-style space-bounded model with O(log(nt)) work space. [uncertain] exact model details of Belova et al. 2024
randomized_or_deterministic: Randomized (Monte Carlo family): the top space bounds (Belova et al. 2024; Nederlof-Wegrzycki 2021) are randomized with small error probability. Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas is randomized under the random-bits assumption. Kane's log-space algorithm is deterministic. [uncertain] exact one-sidedness / success-probability statement of Belova et al.
time_space_tradeoff_curve: The best reduced-space result is essentially a single point: time O*(2^{0.5n}), space O*(2^{0.246n}). More broadly there is a tradeoff family. Schroeppel-Shamir: O*(2^{0.5n}) time, O*(2^{0.25n}) space. Jin-Vyas (SODA 2021): fast low-space algorithms with an explicit time-space tradeoff, e.g. time 2^{n/2}/poly(n) at roughly 2^{n/4} space and polynomial-space variants. Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas: O*(2^{0.86n}) time at polynomial space. Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay (STOC 2019) give SETH-based lower bounds constraining simultaneous low time and low space (when T = S one cannot beat about t^{1-eps} 2^{o(n)}).
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: Space exponent 0.246*n (Belova-Chukhin-Kulikov-Mihajlin, ESA 2024); previous record 0.249999*n (Nederlof-Wegrzycki, STOC 2021); original 0.25*n (Schroeppel-Shamir, FOCS 1979). Time exponent has stayed at 0.5*n since 1979; only polynomial factors were shaved in 2023 (2^{n/2} * n^{-0.5023}, Chen-Jin-Randolph-Servedio).
problem_variant: Vanilla worst-case Subset Sum (decision). The same machinery also applies to Knapsack, k-SUM and binary integer programming with few constraints.
applies_to: Worst-case instances of Subset Sum with n integers and a target t; also Knapsack, k-SUM (Bansal-Garg-Nederlof-Vyas), and Weighted Orthogonal Vectors, which is used as the inner problem by Nederlof-Wegrzycki and Belova et al.
coefficient_set: Not applicable for vanilla Subset Sum, which uses C = {0,1}. The related subset-balancing / generalized subset-sum family uses larger constant coefficient sets C, but that is a different line of work.
density_regime: Density-independent, general worst case. The random-prime / Howgrave-Graham-Joux filtering idea historically targets density around 1 (knapsack cryptanalysis), but the ESA 2024 and STOC 2021 results are stated for arbitrary worst-case instances.
solution_regime: General decision problem (no promise of many solutions). The representation technique still relies on a solution having many representations in the enlarged search space.
cardinality_constraint: No fixed-cardinality constraint. Internally, however, the representation technique splits the search space into Hamming-weight layers and Schroeppel-Shamir enumerates subset sums in cardinality layers, which is what enables the low space bound.
key_technique: Random-prime modular filtering of the family of subsets (Howgrave-Graham-Joux, CRYPTO 2010), combined with Schroeppel-Shamir's low-space sorted sum enumeration and the representation technique; the filtered instance is reduced to many instances of Weighted Orthogonal Vectors.
core_idea: Pick a random prime p and keep only subsets whose sum matches the target modulo p; a genuine solution then has many modular representations, so each filtered smaller instance is easier to solve. Because Schroeppel-Shamir can enumerate subset sums in sorted order using only O*(2^{n/4}) memory, running it inside this filter lowers the space bound while keeping O*(2^{n/2}) time. Belova et al. additionally use the prime-filter structure to simplify and sharpen the analysis, obtaining 0.246n.
reduction_pipeline: Subset Sum -> random-prime modular filter (one instance into many smaller instances) -> Weighted Orthogonal Vectors -> representation-technique combination; Schroeppel-Shamir serves as the inner sum-enumeration primitive.
constructive_vs_existential: Constructive: the algorithms decide feasibility and standard self-reduction recovers the witness. The underlying works prove that a solution is preserved by the modular filter.
search_vs_decision_witness: Primarily decides feasibility; self-reduction yields an explicit witness, and constructivity is established in the works (the filter is designed so that a solution is not lost).
obstacle_to_2n3: These results only reduce space and do not touch the O*(2^{0.5n}) time bottleneck. The algorithms still enumerate or process about 2^{n/2} subset sums (or 2^{n/2} representations), so no parameter choice can push them to O*(2^{n/3}). Reaching 2^{n/3} would require a genuine time breakthrough (beating meet-in-the-middle in time), which space improvements alone cannot provide.
barrier_evidence: Abboud, Bringmann, Hermelin and Shabtay (STOC 2019) prove SETH-based conditional lower bounds for Subset Sum and time-space tradeoffs (when time equals space, t^{1-eps}2^{o(n)} time and space would refute SETH). The O*(2^{n/2}) worst-case time barrier for Subset Sum is a central open problem independent of space.
open_questions: Can the space exponent be pushed below 0.246*n, or all the way to polynomial, while keeping O*(2^{0.5n}) time? Can the time be improved below 2^{n/2} simultaneously with low space? Is there a matching lower bound on the time-space tradeoff for the exact decision problem (analogous to the ABHS lower bounds)? Can the random-prime filter be derandomized?
conditional_hypothesis: SETH is used only for the conditional time-space lower bounds (Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay). The upper-bound space results are unconditional (randomized) and do not rest on lattice, 3-SUM, or k-SUM assumptions.
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: Worst-case guarantees (the algorithms solve all n-integer instances with high probability / no input distribution assumption).
cryptographic_regime: Directly connected to knapsack / subset-sum cryptanalysis at density around 1, where the Howgrave-Graham-Joux representation technique and random-prime filtering originated. However, these are asymptotic complexity upper bounds and do not by themselves constitute a practical attack on concrete cryptosystems.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: Combines with pseudo-polynomial and output-sensitive methods. Bellman's algorithm runs in O(|S(X,t)|*n) and Bringmann-Nakos in O~(|S(X,t)|^{4/3}) (STOC 2020) / Bringmann-Fischer-Nakos in O~(|S(X,t)|*sqrt(n)) (SODA 2025) for the dense, value-sensitive regime, while the space-efficient line mostly targets cryptographically hard low-density / high-value instances.

verification_method: Check the modular-filter lemma and the space-bound proof in the ESA 2024 paper (arXiv:2402.13170); verify the reduction to Weighted Orthogonal Vectors and the Schroeppel-Shamir recurrence; the exponent 0.246 is obtained by numerically optimizing the filter and representation parameters, which a reader can reproduce. Compare with the STOC 2021 exponent 0.249999 and the FOCS 1979 exponent 0.25.
